newsitem.title: JAPAN: Saudi minister to visit Japan, discuss energy.
newsitem.headline: Saudi minister to visit Japan, discuss energy.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's Planning Minister will visit Japan for four days from May 11 to discuss energy issues, the Saudi embassy in Japan said on Friday.
The embassy said Abdul-Wahab bin Abdul-Salam Attar will meet Japanese oil industry officials at a private symposium to be held on May 13.
The symposium will be sponsored by the Committee for Energy Policy Promotion, an arm of the influential business group, the Japan Federation of Economic Organisations (Keidanren).
Attar's visit comes amid market speculation that Saudi Arabia is considering the possibility of not renewing Japan's Arabian Oil Co Ltd's (AOC) concession in the Neutral Zone, local oil traders said.

But an AOC official said the trip was not related to negotiations on the renewal of drilling rights for the company's concession in offshore oilfields in Neutral Zone, which is shared jointly by Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.
"This visit will not address that issue," the AOC official said.

AOC's concession with Saudi Arabia expires in 2000. The AOC, which operates about 160 of the Neutral Zone's 614 wells in the Hout and Khafji fields, produces roughly 315,000 barrels per day (bpd) overall, and has plans to raise output to 350,000 bpd by the end of the century.
"While the Kingdom will probably renew the deal when the time comes, it may make gestures to the contrary in order to get better terms from Japan," an oil industry source said.
Any change in Japan's Neutral Zone arrangement would have serious implications for its crude import regime, traders said.
The Neutral Zone accounted for some 250,000 bpd of Japan's crude needs in the first quarter of this year, according to statistics from Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI).
That represents a 25,000 bpd more than the 1996 average.
Kuwait and Riyadh have equally shared mineral rights in the Neutral Zone since its establishment in 1922 by the sultanate of Nejd, now part of Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait, then a British protectorate.
Kuwait has already agreed in principle to renew AOC's drilling rights, which were due to expire in 2003, for another 30 years.
